title: Credit Risk: Part III & Sovereign Risk
source: Lecture 7 · Credit Risk: Part III & Sovereign Risk

concepts.name: Loan sales: participations and assignments
concepts.definition: The traditional way to transfer credit risk. Participations give the buyer a share with limited contractual control; assignments (90%+ of the US market) transfer all rights. Loans remain hard to sell because each assignment is a bespoke contract.
misconceptions: Thinking a participation transfers full rights

questions.prompt: What's the key difference between a participation and an assignment?
options: An assignment transfers all rights (the buyer becomes the lender); a participation gives the buyer a share with limited contractual control
A participation transfers all rights; an assignment doesn't
questions.explanation: Assignments are the main US contract; participations are common in syndicated loans.
feedback: Participations in syndicated loans are often transferable.

questions.prompt: Which contract type makes up the bulk (90%+) of the US loan sales market?
questions.explanation: In an assignment all rights pass to the buyer.
feedback: CDS are derivatives, not loan sales.

questions.prompt: Who typically buys distressed loans?
options: Investment banks, hedge funds and vulture funds
questions.explanation: They buy cheaply, betting recoveries will be worth more than they paid.
feedback: Not loan sale buyers in the lecture.

questions.prompt: What is a 'good bank–bad bank' model?
options: A troubled bank moves its bad loans into a separate entity, which then sells them off
A bank that lends only to good borrowers
A merger of a healthy bank and a failed one
questions.explanation: It's a major source of distressed loans for sale.

questions.prompt: Why does a buyer of a loan participation effectively face 'double' risk?
options: It's exposed both to the borrower defaulting and to the selling bank failing, because it has limited contractual control
It must pay double the loan amount
It bears interest rate and FX risk on every loan
questions.explanation: In a participation the original bank stays the lender of record, so the buyer depends on it too.

questions.prompt: Why are loans 'essentially not readily marketable', even in the assignment market?
options: Each assignment is a bespoke private contract, with details such as accrued interest settled deal by deal
Assignments only transfer part of the rights
questions.explanation: That complexity is why securitisation and credit derivatives, which create marketable instruments, are seen as advances.
feedback: They can be sold; it's just slow and bespoke.
Many types of buyer hold loans.

questions.prompt: Why have foreign banks been dominant buyers of US-dollar loans?
options: To gain exposure to US borrowers without building a US lending network
Because US loans have no credit risk
questions.explanation: Buying loans gives them the exposure directly.

questions.prompt: A buyer wants full legal rights over a loan and no exposure if the selling bank later fails. Which structure should it use?
options: An assignment: all rights pass to the buyer, which becomes the lender
A participation, because the seller stays the lender of record
questions.explanation: In a participation the buyer has limited control and depends on the seller; an assignment removes that link.
feedback: The issue is rights, not price.
That's exactly the exposure the buyer wants to avoid.
A CDS transfers risk but gives no rights over the loan.

concepts.name: Why banks sell loans, and what holds sales back
concepts.definition: Motives: reduce reserve requirement costs, boost reported (fee) income, meet capital requirements, manage liquidity. Deterrents: borrowers' access to commercial paper, customer relationship effects, informational (lemons) concerns, legal concerns.
misconceptions: Forgetting that selling below book value reduces equity, offsetting the capital benefit

questions.prompt: Which is NOT a motivation for loan sales listed in the lecture?
questions.explanation: The four motives: reserve requirement, reported income, capital requirement and liquidity risk.

questions.prompt: A bank sells a loan that was funded by deposits. What happens to the cost of its reserve requirement (the 'reserve tax')?
questions.explanation: Without the loan, the bank no longer needs those deposits, so it doesn't hold idle reserves against them.
feedback: Selling the loan reduces the deposits it needs.

questions.prompt: How does access to the commercial paper market deter loan sales?
options: Large, creditworthy firms borrow directly from investors, so banks originate fewer high-quality loans to sell
It makes loans illegal to sell
It increases demand for bank loans
questions.explanation: Fewer good loans to sell means less fee income and less to sell for capital, reserve or liquidity reasons.
feedback: It reduces demand for bank loans.

questions.prompt: A bank funds an $80m loan entirely with deposits; the reserve requirement is 8% and the bank could earn 4% on idle funds. How much does selling the loan save each year?
questions.explanation: Reserves = 8% × $80m = $6.4m; forgone return = 4% × $6.4m = $256,000.
feedback: That's the reserves themselves, not their annual cost.
That's 4% of the whole loan; only the reserves sit idle.
That's off by a factor of ten.

questions.prompt: A bank has $8m of capital and $100m of risk-weighted assets. It sells loans with $20m of risk-weighted assets at book value. What is its new capital ratio?
feedback: That ignores the fall in RWA.
That cuts capital instead of RWA.

questions.prompt: How do credit ratings on loans offered for sale help loan sales?
options: They reduce informational concerns (buyers fearing 'lemons'), shrinking the discount buyers demand
They transfer legal risk to the agency
questions.explanation: Independent assessment reassures buyers they aren't being sold the worst loans.
feedback: Agencies don't take on legal risk.

questions.prompt: A borrower discovers its loan has been sold to another party. What risk does the selling bank face?
options: The borrower may take future business elsewhere, so the bank gains fees now but loses income later
The loan returns automatically to the bank
None: the sale removes all links
questions.explanation: Customer relationship effects: sale → upset borrower → lost future business. That's why banks often keep servicing the loan.
feedback: Not affected by the customer's view.

questions.prompt: A bank with $8m capital and $100m RWA sells loans with $20m RWA, but at a $1m loss because buyers fear 'lemons'. What is its new capital ratio?
questions.explanation: Capital falls to $7m and RWA to $80m: 7 ÷ 80 = 8.75%. The loss partly undoes the capital relief.
feedback: That ignores the loss on sale.
That divides by the old RWA (7 ÷ 100).

questions.prompt: A buyer later claims misrepresentation and forces the seller to take the loan back. Which benefits of the sale are lost?
options: The capital and reserve benefits, because the loan and its risk return to the bank, and legal costs eat into fee income
None, because the sale already happened
questions.explanation: Legal concerns: the benefits only hold if the loan is truly gone.
feedback: More than the fee is affected.
Putting the loan back reverses the benefits.
Capital and reserve relief go too.

concepts.name: Asset securitisation
concepts.definition: Loans are pooled and transferred to a separate SPV, which issues securities (pass-throughs, asset-backed bonds, CMOs/CDOs in tranches). Both the loans and the risk leave the bank. Motives: duration, liquidity, capital, funding and fee income. Credit enhancement: LMI (LVR > 80%), guarantees, credit derivatives.
misconceptions: Thinking losses hit Class A first
Thinking the bank can own or control the SPV

questions.prompt: How do securitisation and credit derivatives differ in what leaves the bank?
options: Securitisation removes both the loans and the risk; credit derivatives remove only the risk, and the loan stays on the books
Both remove the loans and the risk
Credit derivatives remove the loans; securitisation only the risk
questions.explanation: Securitisation is a cash instrument; credit derivatives are derivative instruments.
feedback: With a credit derivative the loan stays.

questions.prompt: Why must the SPV be separate from the bank?
options: So the assets have genuinely been sold: the bank may manage it for a fee but can't own or control it, and doesn't consolidate it
So the bank can keep the loans' income
Because only SPVs can issue loans
questions.explanation: The SPV is usually a trust holding the assets for investors, the beneficial owners.

questions.prompt: A bank securitises a pool of loans. What happens to its risk-weighted assets and capital requirement?
questions.explanation: The loans leave the balance sheet, so risk-weighted assets and the capital requirement fall.
feedback: The loans no longer count towards RWA.

questions.prompt: In a CDO structured by default risk, which class absorbs credit losses first?
options: The subordinated class (e.g. Class C), which is in effect quasi-equity
questions.explanation: Payments go A → B → C; losses hit C → B → A.
feedback: Class A is the most senior.

questions.prompt: How is any profit on the sale of loans into a securitisation recorded?
questions.explanation: Ongoing management fees are fee income; profit on the sale is trading income.
feedback: The bank no longer earns the loans' interest.

questions.prompt: When does lenders mortgage insurance (LMI) generally apply as credit enhancement?
options: When the borrower is a company
questions.explanation: The two main Australian providers were Genworth and QBE.

questions.prompt: A CMO is structured by repayment risk. When underlying mortgages are repaid early, who is repaid first?
questions.explanation: Class B isn't repaid until all of Class A is, and so on. CMOs reallocate prepayment risk; CDOs reallocate default risk.

questions.prompt: Class C makes up 5% of a CDO pool and 3% of the pool defaults. Which classes lose money?
options: Classes A, B and C equally
questions.explanation: Class C absorbs losses first; a 3% loss fits inside its 5% layer.
feedback: Class A is protected by the classes below it.
Class B is only hit once Class C is exhausted.

questions.prompt: Which is NOT a motive for securitisation listed in the lecture?
questions.explanation: Securitisation reduces risk-weighted assets.

questions.prompt: Class C is 5% of a CDO pool and Class B is the next 15%; the rest is Class A. If 8% of the pool defaults, what share of Class B's value is lost?
questions.explanation: Class C absorbs the first 5%; the remaining 3% hits Class B: 3 ÷ 15 = 20%. Class A is untouched.
feedback: Class C is only 5%, so B takes the rest.
That's 8 ÷ 15: Class C absorbs the first 5%.
That's the pool loss, not B's share.

questions.prompt: A bank with a positive duration gap securitises its longest-duration mortgages and holds the cash. What happens to its duration gap?
options: It narrows: the long-duration assets leave and cash has near-zero duration, so asset duration falls
It widens, because cash has a long duration
No change: securitisation doesn't affect duration
It narrows, because liabilities get longer
questions.explanation: Securitisation → long-duration assets out, cash in → D_A ↓ → duration gap narrows.
feedback: The lecture lists duration management as a motive.

concepts.name: Credit derivatives: TROR swaps and CDS
concepts.definition: No principal is exchanged and ownership doesn't change. TROR swap: the protection buyer pays the total return on a risky asset and receives LIBOR + spread plus compensation for losses. CDS: the buyer pays a premium and is paid only if a credit event occurs. Buying protection removes credit risk; selling adds it. Both create counterparty risk.
misconceptions: Thinking a CDS pays out every period

questions.prompt: In a TROR swap or a CDS, what changes hands at the start?
options: No principal and no ownership: the contract only sets a notional amount
The full principal of the loan
questions.explanation: Only the risk moves; the asset stays where it is.

questions.prompt: In a TROR swap, what does the protection buyer do?
options: Pays the total return on the credit-risky asset and receives LIBOR + spread plus compensation for losses
Receives the total return and pays LIBOR + spread
Pays a premium and is paid only on default
Buys the asset from the seller
questions.explanation: The buyer effectively goes short the asset without losing ownership.

questions.prompt: In a credit default swap, when does the protection seller pay?
options: Only if a specified credit event (e.g. default) occurs
questions.explanation: The buyer pays the swap spread; the seller makes the credit event payment.
feedback: It pays on a credit event.

questions.prompt: A bank sells CDS protection on a company it doesn't lend to. What happens to its credit risk exposure?
questions.explanation: Selling protection adds the asset's credit risk to the portfolio, with no funding needed.
feedback: The bank is now exposed if that company defaults.

questions.prompt: Which CDS tenor is usually the most liquid?
questions.explanation: Terms are generally one year and longer, with the 5-year tenor the most liquid.
feedback: Liquidity falls again at long tenors.

questions.prompt: What new risk does a CDS create for both parties?
questions.explanation: Each side depends on the other paying what it owes.

questions.prompt: A TROR swap includes a cap on LIBOR + spread. Whom does it protect?
options: The protection seller, who pays LIBOR + spread
questions.explanation: A cap limits what the payer pays; a floor protects the receiver (the buyer).
feedback: The buyer is protected by a floor.
The borrower isn't party to the swap.

questions.prompt: According to AFMA data, which credit derivatives dominate Australian turnover?
options: Basket swaps/credit indices and CDS; TROR swaps are tiny
questions.explanation: E.g. 2011–12: basket swaps and indices about $290bn, CDS about $121bn, TROR about $0.2bn.

questions.prompt: A bank has a large exposure to one mining company and wants to cut it without selling the loan or upsetting the client. What's the best tool?
options: Buy CDS protection on the borrower: the credit risk moves while the loan stays on the books (adding counterparty risk)
Sell CDS protection on the borrower
questions.explanation: Buying protection reduces concentration in one name without a sale the client would notice.
feedback: Moves the loan off the books, which the client may notice.

questions.prompt: A bank holds a bond and has bought protection through a TROR swap. The issuer is downgraded and the bond's price falls. What happens?
options: The bond's total return turns negative, the seller pays LIBOR + spread plus compensation for the loss, so the buyer is hedged
The buyer bears the full loss
The seller now owns the bond
questions.explanation: Downgrade → bond value ↓ → total return negative → seller covers losses → the buyer's position is protected.
feedback: That's what the swap protects against.

concepts.name: Sovereign risk
concepts.definition: A government may restrict or block repayment to foreign creditors regardless of the borrower's credit quality, with limited legal remedies. Lending abroad is a two-step decision. Sovereign ceiling: no borrower is usually rated above its sovereign. Events: rescheduling (most common), forgiveness, repudiation (rare).
misconceptions: Treating a strong borrower as safe regardless of its country

questions.prompt: How does sovereign risk differ from credit risk?
options: A government can restrict or block repayment to foreign creditors regardless of the borrower's own credit quality, with limited legal remedies
Sovereign risk only affects loans to governments
Sovereign risk is just credit risk with a higher rate
questions.explanation: Repayment depends on the borrower's ability and willingness and on the government allowing it.
feedback: It affects private borrowers in that country too.
It's a separate layer of risk.
Sovereign risk adds a government layer.

questions.prompt: What is the sovereign ceiling effect?
options: No borrower in a country is usually rated better than its sovereign
Banks can't lend more than a set amount to foreign governments
The highest possible rating is AAA
questions.explanation: The government can override any private borrower's ability or willingness to pay foreign creditors.

questions.prompt: Which is the most common form of sovereign risk event?
questions.explanation: Rescheduling changes contractual terms such as maturity and interest, e.g. South Korea 1998, Argentina 2001, Greece.
feedback: Reserved for the most severe cases.

questions.prompt: How does the lecture define debt repudiation?
options: The borrower's outright cancellation of all current and future debt obligations: since WWII, only China, Cuba and North Korea
Changing a loan's maturity and interest rate
Lenders agreeing to cancel part of the debt
questions.explanation: It's rare; rescheduling is far more common.
feedback: That's forgiveness, decided by the lenders.

questions.prompt: A country's government becomes more likely to default. Under the sovereign ceiling, what happens to the best rating its companies can achieve?
questions.explanation: Companies are usually rated no better than their sovereign, so a weaker sovereign pulls the ceiling down.
feedback: The ceiling moves with the sovereign.
The ceiling is set by the sovereign's risk.

questions.prompt: Which firm might be rated above its host country's sovereign?
options: A multinational subsidiary whose parent is headquartered in a much lower-risk country
Any firm with strong cash flows
questions.explanation: That's the exception to the sovereign ceiling.
feedback: Strong cash flows don't stop capital controls.

questions.prompt: Lending to a firm abroad is a two-step decision. What are the steps?
options: Assess the borrower's credit quality, then the sovereign risk of its country
Check the exchange rate, then the interest rate
Assess sovereign risk, then ignore the borrower
Check collateral, then the loan size
questions.explanation: Both must be acceptable.

questions.prompt: Why have most international debt problems since WWII been reschedulings rather than outright defaults?
options: Debts were mostly bank loans (few lenders), syndicates of the same FIs were cohesive, and cross-default provisions prevented selective defaults
Governments are legally barred from defaulting
questions.explanation: Fewer, cohesive lenders make negotiating new terms easier.
feedback: Bonds involve many dispersed holders, which is harder.

questions.prompt: In 2011 Hungary let borrowers repay Swiss-franc mortgages at exchange rates about 25% below market. Why is this sovereign risk rather than credit risk?
options: The government changed the repayment terms to foreign lenders, regardless of borrowers' ability to pay
Hungarian borrowers became unable to pay
The banks' collateral fell in value
questions.explanation: Banks lost about US$1.7bn and accused Hungary of expropriation.

questions.prompt: Why are lenders such as the IMF and World Bank willing to forgive the debts of the poorest countries?
options: Forgiveness, conditional on poverty-reduction reforms, avoids outright repudiation
To raise their own credit ratings
questions.explanation: Unlike rescheduling and repudiation, forgiveness is decided by the lenders.

questions.prompt: A healthy exporter in a country that imposes capital controls owes a foreign bank. What happens to the loan?
options: The government blocks foreign-currency payments, so the borrower can't pay despite its strong finances, and the loan may be rescheduled or impaired
It's repaid as normal because the borrower is healthy
The bank can sue the government and recover in full
questions.explanation: Government restriction → payment blocked → default or rescheduling unrelated to the firm's own credit quality. Legal remedies are limited.
feedback: Its ability to pay doesn't matter if payment is blocked.

questions.prompt: A bank is considering a loan to a domestic firm rated AA in a country whose sovereign is rated BB. How should it treat the loan's risk?
options: As no better than BB: under the sovereign ceiling the government can block repayment whatever the firm's strength
As AA, because the firm's own credit quality is what matters
As halfway between AA and BB
As risk-free if the firm exports
questions.explanation: Two-step decision: the firm passes step one, but the sovereign step caps the risk. Only subsidiaries of parents in safer countries are usual exceptions.
feedback: Exporters can still be hit by capital controls.

concepts.name: Country risk evaluation
concepts.definition: Outside ratings (Euromoney, EIU, Institutional Investor); internal statistical models using ratios (DSR, import ratio, investment ratio, export variance, money growth) to separate reschedulers; market data (secondary LDC debt prices); and a combined approach regressing prices on ratios.
misconceptions: Assuming every country-risk scale has 100 = safest

questions.prompt: On the Euromoney Index, what does a score of 100 mean?
questions.explanation: Euromoney combines economic and political factors on a 0–100 scale.

questions.prompt: What's the main drawback of outside country-risk ratings?
options: They aren't tailored: every bank gets the same rating regardless of its own exposures
questions.explanation: They are cheap and allow comparisons, but they're one-size-fits-all and may reflect a narrow view.

questions.prompt: A country's exports fall while its debt payments are unchanged. What happens to its debt service ratio?
questions.explanation: Exports are the denominator, so the DSR rises, and so does the probability of rescheduling.
feedback: A smaller denominator raises the ratio.

questions.prompt: A country's investment ratio (real investment ÷ GNP) rises. What usually happens to its probability of rescheduling?
questions.explanation: The lecture gives a 'likely negative' link: more investment builds future productive capacity.
feedback: The investment ratio's link is likely negative.
It's one of the model's ratios.

questions.prompt: A country's domestic money supply growth (ΔM/M) rises. What happens to its probability of rescheduling?
questions.explanation: Positive link: faster money growth signals inflation, weakening the currency and economy.
feedback: It's one of the model's ratios.

questions.prompt: Which outside rating uses a 100-point scale where 100 = MAXIMUM risk?
questions.explanation: Euromoney and Institutional Investor both use 100 = no risk / no default possibility.

questions.prompt: A country pays $2bn in interest and $3bn in amortisation, and exports $20bn. What is its debt service ratio?
Which problem of statistical country-risk models concerns strikes, corruption and elections?
options: Political risk factors aren't captured by most models
questions.explanation: The Corruption Perceptions Index is one way to bring this in.
feedback: That's about finer distinctions between countries.
That's about the costs and benefits of default.

questions.prompt: Why do statistical models' country-by-country approaches miss part of the risk?
options: They ignore diversification: they should separate the systematic (cross-country) component of default risk from the country-specific one
questions.explanation: This is the 'portfolio aspects' criticism.

questions.prompt: Using the combined approach, a country's LDC debt trades well below the price predicted from its ratios. What does this suggest?
options: Extra risk not captured by the ratios, often political
The debt is underpriced and safe to buy
The model's ratios are all wrong
The country is about to repudiate
questions.explanation: The regression predicts a price from the ratios; a lower actual price signals something extra worrying investors.
feedback: The market is pricing in more risk.
It signals extra risk, not a broken model.

questions.prompt: Which ratios did the market-data approach find significantly affect LDC loan prices?
options: Debt service ratio, import ratio, accumulated debt in arrears, and loan loss provisions against LDC loans
Investment ratio and money supply growth only
questions.explanation: The approach faces the same criticisms as statistical models.

concepts.name: Dealing with sovereign risk exposure
concepts.definition: Loan sales (cost: the loss; benefit: freed resources and a strength signal), loan-for-bond swaps such as Brady bonds (marketable and collateralised, but longer maturity and less than $1 of bond per $1 of loan), debt-for-equity swaps, and multiyear restructuring agreements (MYRAs). Concessionality = PV given up in a MYRA.
misconceptions: Forgetting a loan-for-bond swap gives less than $1 of bond per $1 of loan

questions.prompt: What is concessionality in a MYRA?
options: The amount a bank gives up in present-value terms as a result of the restructuring
questions.explanation: It depends on the fee, rate, grace period, maturity and options.

questions.prompt: What's the main cost of selling an LDC loan?
questions.explanation: The benefits are removal from the balance sheet and a signal of strength.

questions.prompt: In a MYRA, the bank charges a higher restructuring fee and everything else is unchanged. What happens to concessionality?
questions.explanation: The fee offsets part of what the bank gives up, so concessionality falls.
feedback: The fee works in the bank's favour.
The fee is one of the terms that sets it.

questions.prompt: What are the benefits and costs of loan-for-bond swaps such as Brady bonds?
options: Bonds are marketable and liquid, and Brady bonds are collateralised and usually senior; but they have longer maturities and give less than $1 of bond per $1 of loan
They remove all sovereign risk at no cost
They shorten maturities but are illiquid
They give more than $1 of bond per $1 of loan
questions.explanation: Low transaction costs, small bid-ask spreads and efficient settlement make bonds easier to sell.

questions.prompt: Why can selling an LDC loan at a loss send a positive signal?
options: It shows the rest of the balance sheet is strong enough to absorb the loss
It means the loan was worthless
It ends the bank's exposure to all countries
questions.explanation: That signalling effect is listed as a benefit.

questions.prompt: In a MYRA, the new loan's maturity is lengthened and its interest rate cut. What happens to concessionality?
questions.explanation: Both terms lower the present value of what the bank will receive, so it gives up more.
feedback: Maturity and rate are key terms.

questions.prompt: A bank swaps $100m of LDC loans for Brady bonds. Which outcome is consistent with the lecture?
options: It receives less than $100m face value in bonds but gains a marketable, collateralised, usually senior claim with a longer maturity
It receives more than $100m in bonds
questions.explanation: A loan-for-bond swap trades face value for marketability and seniority.
feedback: Collateral is full or partial; risk remains.
